claim: CAF-1 is conserved in all eukaryotes.
source: Discovered over 30 years ago (Smith and Stillman, 1989), conserved in all eukaryotes (Loyola and Almouzni, 2004), the histone chaperone Chromatin Assembly Factor 1 (CAF-1) is central and unique in promoting the deposition of replicative histones H3−H4 in a manner coupled to DNA synthesis
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Loyola and Almouzni, 2004

claim: CAF-1 promotes the deposition of replicative histones H3−H4 in a manner coupled to DNA synthesis.
source: TEXT
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Smith and Stillman, 1989; Loyola and Almouzni, 2004; Ridgway and Almouzni, 2000; Gurard-Levin et al., 2014

claim: CAF-1 is involved in heterochromatin maintenance.
source: the histone chaperone Chromatin Assembly Factor 1 (CAF-1) is central and unique in promoting the deposition of replicative histones H3−H4 in a manner coupled to DNA synthesis, that is during DNA replication and repair, and is also involved in heterochromatin maintenance (see Ridgway and Almouzni, 2000; Gurard-Levin et al., 2014 for review).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ridgway and Almouzni, 2000; Gurard-Levin et al., 2014

claim: CAF-1 provides a link with DNA synthesis via its association with PCNA through PCNA Interacting Protein motifs (PIP).
source: The unique feature of CAF-1 is that it provides a link with DNA synthesis via its association with the trimeric DNA polymerase processivity factor, proliferation cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), through PCNA Interacting Protein motifs (PIP; Martini et al., 1998; Shibahara and Stillman, 1999; Moggs et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2000; Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2009; Pietrobon et al., 2014; Gopinathan Nair et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Martini et al., 1998; Shibahara and Stillman, 1999; Moggs et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2000; Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2009; Pietrobon et al., 2014; Gopinathan Nair et al., 2022

claim: CAF-1 comprises three subunits.
source: CAF-1 comprises three subunits (Figure 1A; Smith and Stillman, 1989; Kaufman et al., 1997; Dohke et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Smith and Stillman, 1989; Kaufman et al., 1997; Dohke et al., 2008, and by Figure 1A showing the three subunits

claim: In S. cerevisiae, CAF-1 is a hetero-trimer that binds to a single dimer.
source: In S. cerevisiae, CAF-1 is a hetero-trimer that binds to a single dimer (Mattiroli et al., 2017a, Sauer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mattiroli et al., 2017a, Sauer et al., 2017

claim: Two domains of the large subunit Cac1 contribute to DNA binding: the KER domain and the C-terminal Winged Helix Domain (WHD).
source: Two domains of the large subunit Cac1 contribute to DNA binding (Zhang et al., 2016; Sauer et al., 2017), the conserved low complexity region called KER (for Lys, Glu, and Arg rich) and the C-terminal Winged Helix Domain (WHD).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2016; Sauer et al., 2017

claim: The DNA binding features of CAF-1 are conserved in human CAF-1.
source: These features are conserved in human CAF-1 (Gopinathan Nair et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gopinathan Nair et al., 2022

claim: The large subunit of CAF-1 exhibits significant sequence divergence across species.
source: The large subunit of CAF-1, present in all major groups of eukaryotes, exhibits significant sequence divergence (16% sequence identity between SpPcf1 and ScCac1 and 21% sequence identity between SpPcf1 and HsCHAF1A/p150, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence identity data and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing sequence alignment

claim: Schizosaccharomyces pombe heterochromatin shares with human a regulation based on the recruitment of Swi6, the heterochromatin function 1 (HP1) orthologue, via histone H3K9 trimethylation.
source: Of particular interest, Schizosaccharomyces pombe heterochromatin shares with human a regulation based on the recruitment of Swi6, the heterochromatin function 1 (HP1) orthologue, via histone H3K9 trimethylation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about S. pombe and human heterochromatin regulation

claim: SpPcf1 is shorter than ScCac1 and HsCHAF1A/p150 (544 residues instead of 606 and 956, respectively).
source: Although SpPcf1 is shorter than ScCac1 and HsCHAF1A/p150 (544 residues instead of 606 and 956, respectively) its sequence includes a remarkable high abundance of predicted Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence length data and Figure 1B showing disorder predictions

claim: SpPcf1 sequence includes a remarkable high abundance of predicted Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs).
source: Although SpPcf1 is shorter than ScCac1 and HsCHAF1A/p150 (544 residues instead of 606 and 956, respectively) its sequence includes a remarkable high abundance of predicted Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1B showing predicted disorder

claim: When isolated, both Pcf2 and Pcf3 are monomeric while Pcf1 forms large soluble oligomers.
source: When isolated, both Pcf2 and Pcf3 are monomeric while Pcf1 forms large soluble oligomers.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from protein purification

claim: Mixing Pcf1 and Pcf2 results in stable complexes.
source: Mixing the subunits by pairs, we observed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC), stable complexes for Pcf1-Pcf2 and Pcf1-Pcf3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Mixing Pcf1 and Pcf3 results in stable complexes.
source: Mixing the subunits by pairs, we observed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC), stable complexes for Pcf1-Pcf2 and Pcf1-Pcf3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Pcf2 and Pcf3 did not interact with each other.
source: Pcf2 and Pcf3 did not interact with each other (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) suggesting that the large subunit Pcf1 mediates the complex assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: The large subunit Pcf1 mediates the complex assembly.
source: Pcf2 and Pcf3 did not interact with each other (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) suggesting that the large subunit Pcf1 mediates the complex assembly.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Pcf2 and Pcf3 do not interact without Pcf1

claim: An experimental molecular weight of 179 kDa was calculated for SpCAF-1 using small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS).
source: An experimental molecular weight of 179 kDa was calculated using small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS).
evidence: The claim is supported by SAXS measurements

claim: The experimental molecular weight of 179 kDa is consistent with a 1:1:1 stoichiometry for the CAF-1 complex (calculated MW 167 kDa).
source: Assuming an accuracy of around 10% with this method (Rambo and Tainer, 2013), this value is consistent with a 1:1:1 stoichiometry for the CAF-1 complex (calculated MW 167 kDa; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SAXS data and comparison with calculated molecular weight, with citation to Rambo and Tainer, 2013 for method accuracy

claim: The SpCAF-1 complex is globular with significant flexibility.
source: In addition, the position of the maximum for the dimensionless Kratky plot was slightly shifted to higher values in the y and x axis compared to the position of the expected maximum of the curve for a fully globular protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D). This shows that the complex was globular with a significant flexibility.
evidence: The claim is supported by Kratky plot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: About 140 amide signals were observed in the 15N-1H spectrum of SpCAF-1(15N-Pcf1), revealing that up to a quarter of Pcf1 residues are intrinsically disordered in the full SpCAF-1 complex.
source: The 15N-1H spectrum shows about 140 amide signals, revealing that up to a quarter of Pcf1 residues are intrinsically disordered in the full SpCAF-1 complex (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The disordered residues in Pcf1 are located in four continuous segments labeled IDR1 to IDR4.
source: These residues are located in four continuous segments of Pcf1 and define Intrinsically Disordered Regions that we labeled IDR1 to IDR4 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data and Figure 1B showing the location of IDRs

claim: IDR1 corresponds to the ~50 N-terminal residues of Pcf1.
source: IDR1 corresponds to the ~50 N-terminal residues of the protein
evidence: The claim is based on NMR data analysis

claim: IDR2 (181-198) is located between the PIP motif and the 3BD region.
source: IDR2 (181-198) is located between the PIP motif and the 3BD region
evidence: The claim is based on NMR data analysis

claim: IDR3 (355-394) overlaps a large segment of the acidic ED domain.
source: IDR3 (355-394) overlaps a large segment of the acidic ED domain
evidence: The claim is based on NMR data analysis

claim: IDR4 (451-470) is located between the 2BD region and the C-terminal WHD domain.
source: IDR4 (451-470) is located between the 2BD region and the C-terminal WHD domain.
evidence: The claim is based on NMR data analysis

claim: The boundaries of the four IDRs are in agreement with the segments of Pcf1 predicted to harbor disorder with a high probability.
source: The boundaries of the four IDRs are in agreement with the segments of Pcf1 predicted to harbor disorder with a high probability (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of NMR data with disorder predictions shown in Figure 1B

claim: The AlphaFold2 model of SpCAF-1 is consistent with biochemical data showing that Pcf1 mediates the complex assembly.
source: The model is consistent with our biochemical data showing that Pcf1 mediates the complex assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of AlphaFold2 model with experimental data

claim: Low pLDDT values around 0.2–0.3 were obtained in the four IDR segments with a remarkable match for the delimitations of the four IDR segments by pLDDT values and NMR data.
source: Also, in agreement with their disordered nature, low values around 0.2–0.3 of the local quality of the model as calculated by the Local Distance Difference Test (pLDDT) were obtained in the four IDR segments with a remarkable match for the delimitations of the four IDR segments by pLDDT values and NMR data (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of AlphaFold2 pLDDT scores with NMR data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The AlphaFold2 model identifies four independent modules in SpCAF-1 that are not predicted to interact with each other.
source: These data allowed to identify four independent modules, not predicted to interact with each other.
evidence: The claim is based on AlphaFold2 modeling results

claim: The first module corresponds to the KER domain of Pcf1, predicted to form a long helix ending by the PIP motif.
source: The first module corresponds to the KER domain of Pcf1, predicted to form a long helix ending by the PIP motif.
evidence: The claim is based on AlphaFold2 modeling results

claim: The second module contains the Pcf2 subunit, composed of 7 WD repeats arranged in a circular fold, and a segment of Pcf1 corresponding to the 2BD domain forming three short beta strands and a short helix.
source: The second module contains the Pcf2 subunit, composed of 7 WD repeats arranged in a circular fold, and a segment of Pcf1 corresponding to the 2BD domain forming three short beta strands and a short helix (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on AlphaFold2 modeling results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: In the third module, the 3BD domain of Pcf1 composed of seven helices and three beta strands establishes a large interface with Pcf3, composed of seven circular WD repeats.
source: In the third module, the 3BD domain of Pcf1 composed of seven helices and three beta strands establishes a large interface with Pcf3, composed of seven circular WD repeats (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is based on AlphaFold2 modeling results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: The fourth domain is the WHD domain.
source: The fourth domain is the WHD domain.
evidence: The claim is based on AlphaFold2 modeling results

claim: The best AlphaFold2 model fitted the experimental SAXS data with high accuracy and is in agreement with a relatively globular complex.
source: The best model fitted the experimental data with a high accuracy and is in agreement with a relatively globular complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of AlphaFold2 model with SAXS data

claim: Superimposing the generated models did not define a unique orientation between the four modules, suggesting that the complex has an inter-module flexibility.
source: Superimposing the generated models did not define a unique orientation between the four modules, suggesting that the complex has an inter-module flexibility (Supplementary file 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–B).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of multiple AlphaFold2 models and SAXS fitting

claim: The large subunit Pcf1 mediates the (1:1:1) complex assembly.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that the large subunit Pcf1 mediates the (1:1:1) complex assembly.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations

claim: Pcf1 includes four IDR, and can organize its key regions (KER, PIP, 3BD, ED, 2BD, and WHD) allowing them to be exposed and bound by Pcf2 and Pcf3 simultaneously.
source: Pcf1 includes four IDR, and can organize its key regions (KER, PIP, 3BD, ED, 2BD, and WHD) allowing them to be exposed and bound by Pcf2 and Pcf3 simultaneously.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on structural and biochemical data

claim: A stable SpCAF-1−H3−H4 complex was isolated by SEC at low (150 mM NaCl) and high (1 M NaCl) salt concentrations.
source: A stable complex was isolated by SEC at low (150 mM NaCl) and high (1 M NaCl) salt concentrations, confirming that the reconstituted SpCAF-1 complex tightly binds histones (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 2A

claim: SAXS measurements at low salt allowed to calculate an experimental molecular weight of 193 kDa for the SpCAF-1−H3−H4 complex, showing that SpCAF-1 binds a dimer of histones H3−H4.
source: SAXS measurements at low salt allowed to calculate an experimental molecular weight of 193 kDa for this complex, showing that SpCAF-1 binds a dimer of histones H3−H4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SAXS measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: The SpCAF-1−H3−H4 complex has a more extended shape compared to SpCAF-1 alone.
source: In addition, these data are compatible with a more extended shape compared to SpCAF-1 alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: Addition of histones to SpCAF-1(15N-Pcf1) led to a drastic decrease in intensity of the NMR signal specifically for residues in the IDR3 segment.
source: Addition of histones to SpCAF-1(15N-Pcf1) led to a drastic decrease in intensity of the NMR signal specifically for residues in the IDR3 segment (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Pcf1_ED (325-396) is fully disordered.
source: We confirmed the fully disordered nature of Pcf1_ED by NMR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: Signals corresponding to residues 355–394 (IDR3) remarkably overlap in the spectra of Pcf1_ED and SpCAF-1(15N-Pcf1), showing that this segment was fully flexible in SpCAF-1.
source: Signals corresponding to residues 355–394 (IDR3) remarkably overlap in the spectra of Pcf1_ED and SpCAF-1(15N-Pcf1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), showing that this segment was fully flexible in SpCAF-1, and did not interact with other regions of the complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectral comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Upon binding of unlabeled histones H3−H4, almost all NMR signals of 15N Pcf1_ED vanished.
source: Upon binding of unlabeled histones H3−H4, we observed the vanishing of almost all NMR signals of 15N Pcf1_ED as in the full SpCAF-1 complex (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Only a shorter fragment (338-347) of Pcf1_ED vanished upon addition of Asf1−H3−H4−Mcm2(69-138).
source: In contrast, only a shorter fragment (338-347) vanished upon addition of Asf1−H3−H4−Mcm2(69-138), a histone complex preformed with two other histone chaperones, Asf1 and Mcm2, known to compete with CAF-1 for histone binding (Sauer et al., 2017) and whose histone binding modes are well established (Figure 2E; Huang et al., 2015; Richet et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR competition experiment and citations to Sauer et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2015; Richet et al., 2015

claim: Residues (325-338) and (349-396) within the ED domain compete with Asf1/Mcm2 for histone binding.
source: This finding underscores a direct competition between residues (325-338) and (349-396) within the ED domain and Asf1/Mcm2 for histone binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the NMR competition experiment results

claim: The segment (353-385) of Pcf1_ED domain was predicted by AlphaFold2 to interact with histones H3−H4 through the same surface as the one bound by Mcm2.
source: Fully consistent with this NMR competition experiment, the segment (353-385) of Pcf1_ED domain was predicted by AlphaFold2 to interact with histones H3−H4 through the same surface as the one bound by Mcm2 (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by AlphaFold2 modeling shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: Two highly conserved positions in Pcf1, L359 and F380, are proposed to mediate histone H3−H4 binding in the same region as Mcm2.
source: Two highly conserved positions in Pcf1, L359 and F380, are thus proposed to mediate histone H3−H4 binding in the same region as Mcm2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is based on AlphaFold2 modeling and sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: All generated SAXS models show a significant exclusion of the KER domain from the SpCAF-1−H3−H4 complex, suggesting that the KER domain of SpCAF-1 becomes more accessible upon histone binding.
source: Remarkably, all generated models show a significant exclusion of the KER domain from the complex, suggesting that the KER domain of SpCAF-1 becomes more accessible upon histone binding.
evidence: The claim is based on SAXS modeling results and inference about KER domain accessibility

claim: An additional region of Pcf1_ED domain (338-351) is involved in the interaction with H3−H4 but is not competing with the Asf1-Mcm2 module.
source: The NMR competition experiment also reveals that an additional region of Pcf1_ED domain (338-351) is involved in the interaction with H3−H4 but is not competing with the Asf1-Mcm2 module (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on NMR competition experiment shown in Figure 2D

claim: The isolated Pcf1_ED* domain (with Y340A and W348A mutations) showed almost no histone binding.
source: As expected, the isolated Pcf1_ED* domain showed almost no histone binding as observed by the intensity of 1H-15N NMR signals (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The full length SpCAF-1 complex with Pcf1-ED* mutations showed no major change upon addition of unlabeled histones H3−H4, strongly suggesting an alteration of the histone binding of this mutant.
source: The 1H-15N NMR spectrum of this mutant was similar to that of the WT complex, but upon addition of unlabeled histones H3−H4 no major change was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which strongly suggest an alteration of the histone binding of this mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Addition of histones leads to a conformational change in the SpCAF-1 complex with less disorder in the ED domain and an increased accessibility of the KER domain.
source: In summary, we identified critical amino-acids in the ED domain involved in H3−H4 binding. We also showed that addition of histones leads to a conformational change in the SpCAF-1 complex with less disorder in the ED domain and an increased accessibility of the KER domain.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on NMR and SAXS data

claim: SpCAF-1 showed significant binding for DNAs longer than 40 bp.
source: The complex SpCAF-1 showed significant binding for DNAs longer than 40 bp (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: When increasing the SpCAF-1 concentration with 40 bp dsDNA, additional mobility shifts suggest a cooperative DNA binding.
source: When increasing the SpCAF-1 concentration, additional mobility shifts suggest, a cooperative DNA binding (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3A

claim: MicroScale thermophoresis (MST) measurements with 40 bp dsDNA showed an EC50 value of 0.7±0.1 µM and a cooperativity (Hill coefficient, h) of 2.7±0.2 for SpCAF-1.
source: The curves were fitted with a Hill model (Tso et al., 2018) with a EC50 value of 0.7±0.1 µM (effective concentration at which a 50% signal is observed) and a cooperativity (Hill coefficient, h) of 2.7±0.2, in line with a cooperative DNA binging of SpCAF-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by MST measurements and fitting with Hill model, with citation to Tso et al., 2018

claim: The isolated Pcf1_KER domain forms a straight monomeric helix, partially continuing over the PIP motif.
source: Using a combination of circular dichroism (CD; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C), SEC-SAXS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and NMR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F), we confirmed that the isolated KER domain of Pcf1 domain forms a straight monomeric helix, partially continuing over the PIP motif.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple biophysical techniques: CD, SAXS, and NMR

claim: Almost all basic residues in the KER helix are positioned on the same side of the helix providing a suitable interface for DNA binding.
source: This long helix exhibits a strong bias in amino acid composition and remarkably, almost all basic residues are positioned on the same side of the helix (Figure 3C) providing a suitable interface for DNA binding (Gopinathan Nair et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3C and citation to Gopinathan Nair et al., 2022

claim: Pcf1_KER domain binds DNA that are longer than 40 bp.
source: We performed EMSA using a DNA ladder as substrate and we found that Pcf1_KER domain binds DNA that are longer than 40 bp, as observed with the full SpCAF-1 complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A

claim: EMSAs with double strand 40 bp DNA fragment showed the presence of multiple bands for Pcf1_KER bound DNA, indicating a possible cooperative DNA binding of this fragment.
source: EMSAs with double strand 40 bp DNA fragment showed the presence of multiple bands for Pcf1_KER bound DNA, indicating a possible cooperative DNA binding of this fragment (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Affinity measurements by MST led to a EC50 of 1.1±0.2 µM for Pcf1_KER with a cooperativity around 3.
source: Affinity measurements by MST led to a EC50 of 1.1±0.2 µM for Pcf1_KER with a cooperativity around 3, consistent with EMSA experiments (Figure 3E, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST measurements shown in Figure 3E and Table 1

claim: The DNA binding properties of Pcf1_KER-PIP are comparable to that of Pcf1_KER.
source: The DNA binding properties of Pcf1_KER-PIP are comparable to that of Pcf1_KER (Figure 3E, Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST and EMSA data shown in Figure 3E, Table 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: The EC50 obtained for the isolated Pcf1_KER are close to that of the full SpCAF-1 complex (0.7±0.1 µM) suggesting that the KER domain constitutes the principal DNA binding domain of SpCAF-1.
source: The EC50 obtained for the isolated Pcf1_KER are also close that of the full SpCAF-1 complex (0.7±0.1 µM) suggesting that the KER domain constitutes the principal DNA binding domain of SpCAF-1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of EC50 values

claim: Pcf1_KER* (with R147E-K150E-K154E-R161E-K168E mutations) is mainly helical.
source: The CD analysis of Pcf1_KER* shows this mutant is mainly helical (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by CD data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: The mutation of Pcf1_KER* impaired DNA binding by a factor of 10 although residual DNA binding remained.
source: MST quantification confirmed that the mutation of Pcf1_KER* impaired DNA binding by a factor of 10 eventhough residual DNA binding remained (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST data shown in Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F, and Table 1

claim: SpCAF-1-KER* showed a lower affinity for dsDNA and a lower binding cooperativity compared to WT.
source: The KER* mutation was then introduced in the full complex SpCAF-1-KER* (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) and we confirmed by MST and EMSA its lower affinity for dsDNA (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, Table 1). Importantly, this mutant also shows a lower binding cooperativity for DNA binding, as estimated by the Hill coefficient value close to 1, compared to values around 3 for the WT and other mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by MST and EMSA data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, and Table 1

claim: The KER* mutation did not impair histone binding.
source: In addition, the NMR signals of all IDR for this mutant with or without histones were close to that of the WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B) indicating that the KER* mutation did not impair histone binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B

claim: The global fold of Pcf1_WHD is similar to ScWHD.
source: We next isolated the Pcf1_WHD domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and confirmed by NMR and AlphaFold2 that its global fold is similar to ScWHD (Liu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR and AlphaFold2 modeling, with citations to Liu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016

claim: Pcf1_WHD does not interact with DNA of any size.
source: Unexpectedly, Pcf1_WHD does not interact with DNA of any size (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B

claim: The residues involved in DNA binding in ScWHD, K564, and K568, correspond to S514 and G518 in SpWHD, leading to a different electrostatic surface, probably not favorable for DNA binding.
source: The residues involved in DNA binding in ScWHD, K564, and K568, correspond to S514 and G518 in SpWHD, respectively, leading to a different electrostatic surface, probably not favorable for DNA binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison and structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C–D

claim: SpCAF-1-ΔWHD showed similar DNA binding property and IDR properties as the WT complex.
source: We observed the similar DNA binding property and IDR properties for SpCAF-1-ΔWHD and the WT complex (Table 1, Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by MST, EMSA, and NMR data shown in Table 1, Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B

claim: The KER domain constitutes the main DNA binding region of SpCAF-1 and the WHD domain does not contribute to this binding.
source: Together our results show that the KER domain constitutes the main DNA binding region of SpCAF-1 and that the WHD domain does not contribute to this binding.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple DNA binding experiments

claim: An affinity of 7.1±1.3 µM was measured between SpPCNA and a short PIP motif segment by ITC.
source: We first measured by isothermal microcalorimetry (ITC) an affinity of 7.1±1.3 µM between SpPCNA and a short PIP motif segment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Table 2

claim: The affinity of Pcf1_PIP for SpPCNA is in the same range (twofold less affinity) as a peptide isolated from the replicative polymerase delta from S. pombe Cdc27.
source: This affinity is in the same range (twofold less affinity) as a peptide isolated from the replicative polymerase delta from S. pombe Cdc27 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Table 2

claim: The binding mode of Pcf1_PIP motif to SpPCNA is predicted by AlphaFold to be canonical.
source: In agreement with its consensus sequence, the binding mode of Pcf1_PIP motif to SpPCNA is predicted by AlphaFold to be canonical (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on AlphaFold2 modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: No binding was observed for the Pcf1_PIP* peptide with 4 Alanine mutations to SpPCNA.
source: Consistently, no binding was observed for the Pcf1_PIP* peptide with 4 Alanine mutations, previously designed to disrupt the PIP motif (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Table 2; Pietrobon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Table 2, with citation to Pietrobon et al., 2014

claim: The affinity of Pcf1_KER-PIP for SpPCNA showed an affinity gain of a factor 10 (0.7±1.3 μM) compared to the short PIP peptide.
source: We next measured the affinity of the longer fragment Pcf1_KER-PIP for SpPCNA and observed an affinity gain of a factor 10 (0.7±1.3 μM; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Table 2), revealing interactions between the KER domain and PCNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Table 2
